prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep topological insulators as my preferred configuration after the full first-round exchange. The discovery is a new class of quantum matter defined by a bulk invariant and protected boundary states, and the chain from idea to observation is direct: Kane and Mele's Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall proposal, then the observation of helical edge transport in HgTe wells by Molenkamp's group. Two decades of work in 2D and 3D materials, with transport and ARPES, and a first-principles band-inversion picture that predicts which compounds are topological, make this both mature and reproduced. That last point is where my own field meets the discovery. Nothing in round 1 has changed my reading of the science. What round 1 has changed is how I word the credit: the citation should name the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation, and the committee should say openly that it does not allocate the whole field.
statement.case_against: The credit gap is the serious problem and I do not want to minimise it. Bernevig, Hughes and the late Zhang made the HgTe/CdTe proposal that Molenkamp's experiment tested, and the 3D work of Fu, Moore, Balents, Hsieh and Hasan sits outside any three names; Zhang's death means this cannot be repaired later. Edge quantisation in HgTe is also less clean than in the quantum Hall effect, and the 2016 prize on topological phases is adjacent. Against that, B037 offers the cleanest two-name credit on the shortlist and is preferred by five colleagues, so I have to ask whether an incomplete but defensible credit on a mature topic should outweigh a clean credit on a topic where the novelty relative to 2005 and 2012 is contested. I conclude that it should, narrowly, but I regard this as a close call and not a settled one.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the optical lattice clock rests on one identifiable idea, Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, that the underlying atomic physics (polarisabilities, blackbody and other shifts) is well understood and independently reproduced, and that the neutral-atom clock fills a gap left by the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my position and I take it seriously. I asked in round 1 for a view on novelty from someone who can judge the systematics, and you have given one: the idea is specific, the physics is controlled, and the result is reproduced. That moves B037 from a candidate I could not assess to one I regard as fully prize-worthy, which is why I keep it as my first alternative. It does not change my preference, for one reason. The concern I still cannot resolve is whether the lattice clock is a new principle or an excellent realisation of a precision-measurement programme already honoured twice, and I do not think the committee has answered Mehlig's question about what new principle it adds beyond the magic-wavelength idea. I would not oppose B037 if the committee settles that.

responses.point: Olsson moved to B037 because the credit problems on the other candidates are more serious than she had weighed, while keeping novelty against the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the pending redefinition of the second as reservations.
responses.response: I understand the logic, because it is the same trade-off I face from the other side. The difference is how serious the credit defect is. On B042 the omission is of the authors of the proposal the experiment tested, and of a deceased contributor, which I do accept as the weightier defect. But a clean credit does not by itself make a discovery, and the clock's own risk, a third return to one metrological thread, is a scientific objection and not a bookkeeping one. If the committee finds the Z2 trio indefensible, I would rather move to B037 than force an unfair B042 configuration, and I would support the narrow citation you propose.

responses.point: Pearce, who shares B042 as the preferred part, asks supporters to word a citation that credits the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation while stating openly that the BHZ proposal and the 3D work are outside it, and asks whether the 2016 prize overlaps.
responses.response: I would word it as above: the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells, with an explicit sentence in the committee's popular and scientific background that the BHZ proposal and the 3D work are integral to the field and are not being allocated. On 2016, my view is that the overlap is real but partial: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz concerned integer quantisation and topological transitions in films with broken time reversal, whereas the Z2 insulator is a time-reversal-invariant, spin-orbit-driven state that produced a materials programme. On quantisation, the HgTe edge conductance is near but not cleanly at the expected value in longer channels, so I would keep the experimental half of the citation to the observation of helical edge transport, not to precise quantisation.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B037 because the Higgs credit is arbitrary and nobody calls the Katori-Ye credit unresolved, and he asks whether the pending redefinition of the second and the omitted NIST, PTB and ion-clock groups count against it.
responses.response: Your argument that a defensible allocation matters more than the headline discovery is one I share on B006: the Higgs is the more fundamental result, but I cannot defend three names from two collaborations either. I do not read the omitted groups and the pending redefinition as decisive against B037, and on that I agree with Lindroth and Kroll. Where I differ from you is that B042 has no unresolved allocation of the same kind as B006: the credited names correspond to identifiable first contributions, even if others are missing, whereas for the Higgs no principled rule picks the three.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers active-matter hydrodynamics (B005) as a general nonequilibrium concept, and lists the omission of Yuhai Tu and the still-contested two-dimensional exponents as real defects.
responses.response: I value the generality of the concept, and I agree it is the better physics argument for B005 than a material-specific one. But you name two defects yourself, and I think they weigh more heavily on B005 than the equivalent ones do on B042. Tu is a co-author of the central Toner-Tu theory and the exponents are contested, so the core prediction is not settled. For B042 the omissions are of adjacent contributors, while the core prediction, helical edge states in a Z2 insulator, has been observed and reproduced. For that reason I do not see a route from B005 to a majority, though I accept that this is a judgment about maturity and not about conceptual quality.

responses.point: Johansson now regards B037 as the candidate where merit, attribution and maturity line up most cleanly, and still lists B042 as an alternative while citing the graphene spin-orbit gap and the BHZ and Fu-Moore credit problem.
responses.response: We agree on the facts: the graphene gap is tiny and the credit set is incomplete. I think the question for you and me is whether a defect in the original material proposal matters to the prize, and I do not think it does, since the Z2 concept was realised in HgTe and later in bulk compounds. Your own ranking suggests the credit gap is what keeps B042 from your first choice, and I take that seriously. I would only ask that the committee compare B042 with B037 on the novelty problem as well as on credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize that leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and the late Zhang, or whether that omission is judged too serious; I would move to B037 if it is.

Whether the lattice clock adds a new principle beyond magic-wavelength trapping sufficient for the discovery criterion given the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I cannot judge the systematics myself and rely on Lindroth and Kroll.
How much weight the 2016 prize on topological phases should carry against a quantum spin Hall prize.
I rely on memory for the detailed priority history, including the HgTe edge-conductance data, which I have not verified here.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My field is electronic-structure and magnetism theory, adjacent to topological band theory and to DMFT (B027), but the profile documents no personal or institutional tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Georges, Vollhardt, Kotliar, Katori or Ye. I chaired the 2025 cycle, which concerned a different topic. This disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
